newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian police struggle to stamp out gang war.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian police struggle to stamp out gang war.

text.p: Hungarian police said on Tuesday they were making little headway against an escalating war between gangs whose latest battlefield was a luxury car dealership attacked with hand grenades.
"The entire organised staff of the Budapest police is working on the bombing series, but we are short of manpower," Hungarian police spokesman Mihaily Deszi told Reuters.
Hungary's new national police chief, Attila Berta, told Hungarian radio he expected further attacks linked to what he called a "mafia war associated with the development of society".
At least three people have been killed and almost two dozen car showrooms, restaurants, pubs, nightclubs or peep shows damaged since September by hand grenades or petrol bombs.
Residents of the city of two million people are becoming alarmed by the rash of attacks, which has escalated in recent weeks.
Hand grenades thrown over a chain-link fence into the outdoor lot of the Auto Super dealership in the capital seriously damaged one car and caused minor damage to several others, police said.
They said witnesses saw one or two men running away after the attack on Monday night.
It was the fourth attack in less than a week. A hand grenade bombing in the toilet of a Chinese restaurant on Friday killed the owner's wife and daughter.
Diplomats said the attacks, such as the one at the Chinese restaurant and a petrol-bombing on Monday morning of a Greek-owned country music club, were edging closer to tourist locations.
"It's one thing when they attack a peep show, it's another when it's a mainstream restaurant," one diplomat said.
"It could have a chilling effect" on the tourist industry, he added.
Police have made few arrests and say they have received little cooperation from victims.
The owner of the car dealership, an Afghan who is a naturalised Hungarian, declined to tell reporters his name. "I don't know anything about this," he added.
Other countries in eastern Europe have been hit by an upsurge in crime since the collapse of communism in 1989.
Violent crime has soared in Bulgaria and is worsening with the country's economic collapse. Car bombs are a popular way of settling scores between powerful mafia-type business groups.

In the latest such attack, a former military prosecutor and his wife were badly injured on Monday when a bomb wrecked their car outside their home in the Bulgarian capital Sofia. General Lilko Yotsov worked as an adviser to such a business group after retiring.
Political analysts said societies in transition might experience upsurges in crime, but they were not an excuse for the authorities to throw up their hands in despair.

"I think if sociologists or political scientists say it, that is one thing but if the police chief is going to use that argument it is just not right," said Istvan Stumpf of the Budapest School of Politics.
